newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan CBK says mills seek coffee industry control.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan CBK says mills seek coffee industry control.

text.p: The Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) said on Tuesday that wealthy Kenyans, in the name of competition and transparency in coffee marketing, were seeking to distort sales by central auction and take control of the industry.

CBK Public Relations Manager Paul Kivila told Reuters: "It is a ploy to create room for the wealthy to hijack the industry. All they want is funds from coffee sales to be channelled through them instead of directly to farmers as we are doing."

With 16 billion shillings ($291.4 million) in foreign exchange receipts in 1995/96 (October/September), coffee is Kenya's third largest hard currency earner, behind tourism and tea. Kenya produces mild arabicas that fetch premium prices on the global market.

On Monday, top executives from the Kenya Planters' Cooperative Union (KPCU) and Thika Coffee Mills said they wanted auctions to be retained but the government to give them an option to sell coffee outside the auction if that provided better prices.
KPCU mills around 70 percent of Kenya's total production while Thika Coffee Mills (TCM) has a 10 percent share. KPCU is owned by small coffee growers while TCM is private.
KPCU Board Managing Director James Nyaga and TCM Chairman Pius Ngugi said they sought the option to sell other than via a central auction to encourage competition and transparency.
They said they planned to withhold milled coffee to force the coffee board to agree to their demand for licensing of other companies to join the board in marketing.
Kivila said the millers would be in contravention of the law and agreements with farmers if they withheld milled coffee.
"Withholding of coffee is illegal. Millers do not own coffee and have no powers to effect such action," Kivila said.
"We would like to assure consumers that coffee is available and we shall consistently supply it without any interruptions."
Under Kenyan law, millers hand over all processed coffee to the CBK which sells it at the export auction and passes on payments directly to farmers. CBK pays miller charges directly.

Kivila said KPCU and TCM were licensed to purchase coffee at the central auction for their clients. If the argument was that they could strike better prices outside of the auction, then they should purchase at the auction for resale and make the huge profits, he said.
Answering miller queries over CBK accounts, Kivila said CBK had not published its annual report since 1991/92 due to delays by the office of the state auditor-general for corporations.

But Kivila said auditors KPMG Peat Marwick were given CBK accounts since 1993/94 in February and asked to present a report in six months. CBK was recently exempted from Kenya's State Corporations Act to allow it to enhance its management style and cut government involvement.

This month, President Daniel arap Moi appeared to signal a change in policy, saying millers would be allowed an influential marketing role provided they raised one billion shillings ($18 million) as bail protection against any farmer losses.
But in an unexpected turnaround Moi later said coffee marketing lay under the sole authority of the coffee board and no one should interfere with that mandate.
Kivila said the CBK planned to sell part of its 65 percent shareholding in Kenya Coffee Auctions Ltd to stakeholders. He would not give a date for when that would be done.
